primary_topics: Chapter 13 of 'A Centenary of Justice' -- CJP's analysis of Estrada v. Desierto and Estrada v. Arroyo (decided March 2, 2001, per Puno, J., 13-0), the landmark ruling upholding Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo's succession to the presidency, from which CJ Davide and CJP voluntarily inhibited

Why Arroyo is the de jure President: under the 'totality test,' Estrada had resigned before her noon January 20, 2001 oath (the serialized Angara Diary as the 'authoritative window' on his mind; his final press release a 'valedictory' -- 'his presidency is now in the past tense'); she took her oath as President, not merely acting President, with Congress's recognition

The pivotal distinction between EDSA I and EDSA II: EDSA I was an 'extra-constitutional' revolution that overthrew the whole government (beyond judicial review, per Lawyers League v. Aquino), while EDSA II was 'intra-constitutional' -- an exercise of free speech and assembly that affected only the presidency and is therefore subject to judicial review; 'EDSA I presented a political question; EDSA II involves legal questions'

The spectrum of concurring and separate opinions (Bellosillo, Vitug, Mendoza; Kapunan, Pardo, Santiago, Gutierrez), the 13-0 denial of reconsideration (April 3, 2001), and CJP's own carefully reasoned voluntary inhibition, distinguishing disqualification, inhibition and recusal
sub_topics: The decision and vote: Estrada's petitions dismissed; Arroyo's presidency upheld as de jure by a 13-0 vote (per Puno, J.), with Davide and CJP taking 'no part'

The totality test and resignation: 'the totality of prior, contemporaneous and posterior facts'; the Angara Diary (serialized in the Inquirer) as the 'authoritative window on the state of mind' of Estrada; his final press release acknowledged Arroyo's oath, said he was leaving for peace and reconciliation, and was 'his valedictory, his final act of farewell' -- 'his presidency is now in the past tense'; his claimed 'temporary leave of absence' letter given 'scant legal significance'

Arroyo as President, not acting President: she took her oath as President; House Resolutions 175 and 176 supported her assumption and 178 confirmed Guingona as Vice-President; some twelve senators recognized the new government; the Senate declared the Impeachment Court 'functus officio'; Congress sent bills for her signature
No immunity from suit: Estrada was no longer the sitting president, and 'the unlawful acts of public officials are not acts of the State'; the Court cited Nixon and Clinton v. Jones

The political-question distinction: EDSA I (Lawyers League v. Aquino) was a successful revolution beyond judicial scrutiny because the 1973 Constitution itself had been abrogated; EDSA II did not abolish the 1987 Constitution -- Arroyo swore to preserve it -- so 'EDSA I is extra constitutional... EDSA II is intra constitutional,' the former a political question, the latter involving legal questions subject to review

Concurring opinions: Bellosillo (permanent 'functional' disability viewed objectively -- mass resignations, withdrawal of military/police support, congressional and international recognition -- and subjectively, through Estrada's own statements); Vitug (abandonment of office as a species of resignation; EDSA II was not a revolutionary government because the constitutional structure 'remained intact and functioning'); Mendoza (Estrada 'totally and permanently disabled' by Jan 19; only one government exists, unlike the WWII Quezon-Laurel two-presidents situation)

Separate opinions concurring 'in the result': Kapunan (Estrada was 'virtually forced out,' not a voluntary resignation, yet Arroyo's legitimacy 'is an irreversible fact'); Pardo (joining Mendoza; Estrada 'constrained to resign')

Justice Santiago's disquietude over 'people power': there is 'nothing in the Constitution to legitimize the ouster of an incumbent President' by extra-constitutional means; 'people power' is an 'amorphous and indefinable concept' (even 2 million at EDSA would be only 2.67% of 75 million Filipinos); 'the situation should conform to the Constitution. The Constitution should not be adjusted... to conform to the situation'; she rebukes media pressure on the Court -- yet agrees Arroyo 'rightfully assumed the presidency'

Justice Gutierrez's view: a resignation made 'under duress is voidable,' and Estrada's was not clear or voluntary (he was 'constrained' to leave amid imminent danger), but the legality question was 'laid to rest by the results' -- Arroyo is the de jure President

The 13-0 denial of reconsideration (April 3, 2001): the Court listed twenty-three prior events building the 'irresistible pressure' to resign (from the Singson exposé to the withdrawal of military support); debunked the 'duress' claim (the Palace was protected, 'no tanks... no shooting'); and held the Angara Diary admissible (adoptive admission; admissions of an agent bind the principal; not barred by the hearsay rule)

Denial of mass inhibition and CJP's own inhibition: the twelve justices present at the EDSA Shrine were 'mere spectators' who 'did not prejudge,' and mass disqualification would 'pro tanto' deprive the Court of jurisdiction; CJP's 'Extended Explanation of Inhibition' distinguished compulsory disqualification (Rule 137, Sec. 1) from voluntary inhibition and recusal, and explained he inhibited 'pro hac vice' not for any legal ground but 'to hold myself above petitioner's reproach' -- contrasting the Veterans Federation case, where the Court rejected his offer to inhibit

stances.claim: The legitimacy of Arroyo's succession is a LEGAL, not a political, question -- because EDSA II, unlike EDSA I, was 'intra constitutional': it did not overthrow the government or abrogate the 1987 Constitution but merely caused a sitting President's resignation and the Vice President's constitutional succession, which the Court may review. 'EDSA I presented a political question; EDSA II involves legal questions.'
stances.rhetorical_move: EDSA-I/EDSA-II distinction: drawing a bright line between extra-constitutional revolution (non-justiciable) and intra-constitutional succession (justiciable) to establish the Court's jurisdiction
stances.confidence: the unanimous holding of the Court (13-0)

stances.claim: Estrada effectively resigned before Arroyo's noon oath, as shown by the 'totality' of his prior, contemporaneous and posterior acts -- the Angara Diary revealing his intent, and his final press release functioning as a 'valedictory' in which 'his presidency is now in the past tense'; the office was therefore vacant, and his later claim of mere 'temporary inability' and of resignation 'under duress' cannot stand against the protected, violence-free circumstances of his departure.
stances.rhetorical_move: totality-test plus documentary inference: reconstructing subjective intent from the full evidentiary record (including a diary as adoptive admission) rather than from a single formal act
stances.confidence: the Court's holding, reinforced on reconsideration

stances.claim: A judge's voluntary inhibition is distinct from compulsory disqualification: CJP inhibited himself 'pro hac vice' not because any legal ground of bias existed but 'to hold myself above petitioner's reproach' and to deny anyone an excuse to doubt the integrity of a decision 'of transcendental importance to the nation' -- while the mass disqualification of the twelve 'mere spectator' justices was properly refused, since it would 'pro tanto' deprive the Court of its constitutional jurisdiction.
stances.rhetorical_move: inhibition-vs-disqualification framing: separating discretionary self-recusal (a matter of conscience and appearances) from compulsory legal grounds, and defending the Court's integrity against tactical mass-recusal demands
stances.confidence: asserted by CJP in his Extended Explanation and by the Court on the inhibition issue

notable_anecdotes: 'His presidency is now in the past tense': the Court parsed Estrada's final press release line by line -- his acknowledgment of Arroyo's oath, his leaving 'for the sake of peace,' his gratitude for the 'past opportunity to serve' -- to conclude that the statement was 'his valedictory, his final act of farewell.'

The 2.67% point: in her separate opinion, Justice Ynares-Santiago questioned whether the EDSA throng was truly 'the people,' reasoning that even a generous estimate of 2 million would be only 2.67% of 75 million Filipinos -- warning that 'the situation should conform to the Constitution,' not the reverse.

The twenty-three events: on reconsideration, the Court enumerated twenty-three prior events -- from the Singson exposé and the second-envelope vote to the mass withdrawal of military and Cabinet support -- building the 'irresistible pressure' to resign, noting that 'for all his loud protestations, petitioner has not singled out any of these facts as false.'

No tanks, no shooting: rejecting the duress claim, the Court observed that the Palace was protected by the Presidential Security Guard and that 'no harm, not even a scratch,' befell Estrada, who even detoured to bid goodbye to followers at the San Juan Municipal Hall -- 'no tanks... no shooting... except verbal violence.'

The mirror-image inhibitions: both Davide and CJP voluntarily stepped aside, Davide noting he disagreed with the grounds urged but inhibited 'to dispel any doubt,' and CJP explaining at length that he acted 'pro hac vice... to hold myself above petitioner's reproach' -- contrasting the earlier Veterans Federation case where the Court had refused his offer to inhibit.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 13 of 'A Centenary of Justice' is CJP's detailed analysis of Estrada v. Desierto and Estrada v. Arroyo (decided March 2, 2001, per Puno, J., by a 13-0 vote), the landmark ruling upholding Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo's succession, from which both CJ Davide and CJP voluntarily inhibited. The Court held Arroyo the de jure President: applying the 'totality test,' it found Estrada had resigned before her noon January 20, 2001 oath -- the Angara Diary serving as the 'authoritative window' on his intent and his final press release a 'valedictory' in which 'his presidency is now in the past tense' -- and that she took office as President (not merely acting), with Congress's recognition (House Resolutions 175/176/178), Guingona confirmed as Vice-President, and the Impeachment Court declared functus officio. It denied Estrada immunity (citing Nixon and Clinton v. Jones) and drew its pivotal distinction: EDSA I was an 'extra constitutional' revolution beyond judicial review (Lawyers League v. Aquino), whereas EDSA II was 'intra constitutional' -- an exercise of free speech and assembly affecting only the presidency -- so 'EDSA I presented a political question; EDSA II involves legal questions.' CJP canvasses the concurrences (Bellosillo on permanent 'functional' disability; Vitug on abandonment as resignation and EDSA II as non-revolutionary; Mendoza on Estrada's total disability and the existence of only one government) and the separate opinions concurring 'in the result' (Kapunan and Gutierrez doubting voluntary resignation yet accepting Arroyo's legitimacy as 'an irreversible fact'; Santiago's disquietude over 'people power' -- even 2 million at EDSA being only 2.67% of 75 million Filipinos -- and her insistence that 'the situation should conform to the Constitution'). The 13-0 reconsideration (April 3, 2001) listed twenty-three prior events building the pressure to resign, debunked the 'duress' claim ('no tanks... no shooting'), and upheld the Angara Diary as an adoptive admission. Finally, CJP recounts his own inhibition, distinguishing compulsory disqualification (Rule 137) from voluntary inhibition and recusal, and explaining that he stepped aside 'pro hac vice... to hold myself above petitioner's reproach,' even as the Court rightly refused the tactical mass disqualification of the twelve 'mere spectator' justices.
